sections.heading: Zamindars, palegars and 'little kings' — Andhra's layered old regime

blocks.text: Pre-colonial Andhra authority was a **pyramid of 'little kings'**: Vijayanagara's **nayankara** system had seeded **palegars (palayakkarars)** — warrior chiefs holding forts and revenue rights in the uplands; the coast carried **zamindari houses** (Vizianagaram's Pusapatis, Bobbili's Ranas, Pithapuram, Venkatagiri, Nuzvid) descended from Golconda-Mughal grants; beneath both, village headmen-karanams. The Company **froze one layer and destroyed the other**: coastal zamindars received **permanent sanads (1802-03)** — converted from chiefs into revenue landlords loyal to Madras; the **palegars were crushed** (Munro's Ceded-Districts disarmament, 1800s; the Rayalaseema forts slighted) — ryotwari replaced their world.

rows: **Palegar system**
Fort-based warrior chiefs (kavali/watch fees, blackmail-protection duality); Vijayanagara-Nayaka lineage; Rayalaseema-Nellore belt
Suppressed as 'predatory' — disarmament & pensions (contrast TN's bloody Poligar wars, 1799-1805); their memory lives in **Narasimha Reddy (1846-47)** — a palegar-pension grievance turned rising
**Coastal zamindaris**

Great houses: **Vizianagaram** (the largest; Padmanabham's 1794 defiance), **Bobbili** (the 1757 Bobbili-Vizianagaram-Bussy epic — Tandra Paparayudu's legend), Pithapuram (patron of reform — Venkataratnam Naidu's college), Venkatagiri, Nuzvid, Challapalli
Sanad-fixed revenue; many slid into debt-litigation (Court of Wards); some became **patrons of education-culture** (Vizianagaram's colleges, Pithapuram's reform patronage) — the double face
**Native states & little kings**
**Banganapalle** (Nawabi enclave in Kurnool — a princely state till 1948) and **Sanjeevaraopeta/other petty holdings**; the agency's **muttadars** (hill chiefs under special regulations)
Banganapalle acceded 1948; muttadari abuses fed the fituris (Rampa 1879; Alluri's rising against muttadar-forest oppression)

sections.heading: The system's working — and its dismantling

items: **Inside a zamindari**: the estate as mini-state — kattubadi (quit-rent) chains, village officers, temple-honours patronage, private police; peasant burdens (rasams, vetti-like exactions) exceeding ryotwari rates → the **anti-zamindari ryot movements** of the 1920s-30s (Venkatagiri agitation; **Challapalli & Munagala struggles; N.G. Ranga's organising**) — Andhra's kisan politics was substantially **anti-estate** politics.

**Legal endgame**: Madras Estates Land Act (1908 — tenant-right skeleton) → estates' inquiry committees (1930s Prakasam-era) → **Madras Estates (Abolition & Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948** — the estates taken over, lands resettled as ryotwari; inam abolition followed (1950s legislation) — the old regime's paper death, with compensation politics trailing for decades.

**Assessment**: the 'little kings' were neither pure parasites nor pure patrons — extraction AND education-patronage coexisted (Vizianagaram's music-Sanskrit colleges vs its rent rolls); the exam-ready line: **colonialism first made them landlords, nationalism then unmade them** — and the peasantry paid the toll of both makings.

sections.heading: 🏺 Deep mastery — zamindars, palegars & the 'little kings'

items: **The order:** **palegars/poligars** (military chieftains) and **zamindars** were the intermediary 'little kings' of the Andhra countryside; the **Permanent Settlement (extended to the Circars)** froze them as revenue landlords.

**Resistance & dismantling:** poligar rebellions against Company revenue demands; later the **Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act 1948** dismantled the zamindari system, converting tenants to ryots.
**Social consequence:** sub-infeudation, tenant insecurity and agrarian tension that fed peasant movements — the backdrop to later communist and kisan mobilisation in coastal Andhra & Telangana.
**Significance:** the land question is the connective tissue between colonial Andhra's social structure and its 20th-century radical politics.

prelimsPointers: **Poligars/Palegars** — military chieftains; led early resistance to Company revenue collection.
**Madras Estates Abolition Act 1948** — abolished zamindari in the Andhra region.
**Battle of Bobbili (1757)**: Bobbili vs Vizianagaram-Bussy; **Tandra Paparayudu's** revenge-legend — the Telugu heroic ballad staple.
**Padmanabham (1794)**: Vizianagaram's Chinna Vijayaramaraju fell fighting the Company.
Coastal permanent **sanads issued 1802-03** to Vizianagaram, Pithapuram, Venkatagiri, Nuzvid, Bobbili etc.
**Palegar** = palayakkarar (fort-chief); Munro pacified the Ceded Districts' palegars (1800s).
**Banganapalle** — a Nawab-ruled princely state inside Kurnool region until **1948** accession.
**Muttadar** = agency hill-chief/revenue farmer under the special regulations; muttadari abuse fed **Rampa 1879** and Alluri's rising.
**Madras Estates Land Act 1908**; **Estates Abolition Act 1948** — zamindari's end in Andhra.
**N.G. Ranga's** kisan movement targeted Venkatagiri-type estates — anti-zamindari as Andhra's agrarian politics.
mainsAngles: Colonialism made chiefs into landlords and warriors into pensioners — trace the divergent fates of Andhra's palegars and zamindars.
The zamindari estate was a mini-state — reconstruct its working and the ryot movements it provoked.
From the 1908 Act to the 1948 abolition — narrate the legal dismantling of Andhra's old agrarian regime.
The little kings were extractors and patrons at once — argue the double face with Vizianagaram and Pithapuram.
Link muttadari oppression to the fituri tradition — the agency's variant of the anti-landlord struggle.

glossary.definition: Fort-holding warrior chief of the southern uplands exercising revenue-police powers — the Vijayanagara-Nayaka order's local units.
The engrossed deed by which Madras fixed coastal zamindars' permanent revenue (1802-03) — chiefship converted to landlordism.
Hill-tract chief/revenue intermediary of the Andhra agency under special regulations — the fituris' immediate oppressor tier.
Quit-rent/tribute payable by sub-holders to the zamindar — the estate pyramid's cement.
Colonial trusteeship managing indebted/minor-ruled estates — many Andhra zamindaris passed through it.
Madras Act converting zamindari estates to ryotwari with compensation — the legal end of Andhra's landlord regime.

sections.heading: The pantheon — five makers of modern Andhra

rows: **Kandukuri Veeresalingam (1848-1919)** — 'Gadya Tikkana', the Andhra reformer

*Vivekavardhini* (1874); **Rajahmundry widow-remarriage (11 Dec 1881)**; **Hitakarini Samaj** (his properties willed to it); widows' homes, girls' schools; *Rajasekhara Charitramu* (1878 — first major Telugu novel); *Satyavati Charitram*; prolific satire
The renaissance's engine: reform + prose + press in one person; ~40 remarriages performed against boycott and violence; 'the Vidyasagar of the south'
**Gurajada Apparao (1862-1915)**
*Kanyasulkam* (1892; pref. 2nd ed. 1909); **'Desamunu preminchumanna' (Desabhakti song)**; short stories (*Diddubatu*); Vizianagaram court scholar
Modern Telugu literature's founding play — bride-price, fake sannyasis, the immortal **Gireesham & Madhuravani**; spoken-dialect literature vindicated; 'a nation is its people, not its soil'
**Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu (1862-1939)**
Brahmo missionary-educationist; principal, **Pithapuram Rajah's College (Kakinada)**; 'social purity' movement; knighted; students called him 'Kulapati'
**Anti-nautch & anti-devadasi campaign**, temperance, Dalit-uplift hostels; moulded a generation (his students seeded Andhra's public life)
**Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy (1863-1940)**
*Telugu* (journal); Savara linguistics (first grammar-dictionary of a Munda tongue); the **vyavaharika crusade** vs granthika (Jayanti Ramayya's camp)
Democratised the written language — schoolbooks & press in living Telugu; **Telugu Language Day = his birthday (29 Aug)**; 'Pidugu' (thunderbolt) Gidugu
**Annie Besant (1847-1933)**
(Full portrait HCOI-097) Adyar Theosophy; Home Rule (1916); *New India*
For Andhra specifically: Theosophical lodges as the coastal elite's finishing school; Home Rule's Andhra network (Gadicherla, Kaleswara Rao); the awakening's all-India bridge

items: **Division of labour**: Kandukuri reformed **practice** (marriages performed, homes built), Gurajada reformed **imagination** (the play that made reform laughable-at-orthodoxy), Gidugu reformed the **medium** (language itself), Venkataratnam reformed **character-formation** (the college as reform's seminary), Besant linked it to **all-India politics** — five levers of one awakening.

**Conflict lines worth knowing**: Kandukuri vs orthodox pandits (Kokkonda Venkataratnam's opposition); Gidugu vs **Jayanti Ramayya Pantulu's** granthika camp (the 1910s textbook wars); Besant vs Gandhian mass politics (1919-20) — reform advanced through argument, not consensus.

**Legacy audit**: widow remarriage stayed rare but legitimate; Kanyasulkam's targets (bride-price) faded while its language lived; vyavaharika won totally (all modern Telugu print); the purity movement fed both social reform and (critics note) respectability politics; Besant's network became the Congress cadre — every stream flowed into the Andhra movement (HCOA-062-067).

sections.heading: 🏺 Deep mastery — the makers of modern Andhra

items: **The pantheon:** **Kandukuri Veeresalingam** (social reform), **Gurajada Apparao** (*Kanyasulkam* — anti-bride-price play; 'Desamante Matti Kaadoi, Desamante Manushuloy' — humanist nationalism), **Gidugu Ramamurthy** (the **vyavaharika bhasha / spoken-Telugu movement**), **Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu** (Brahmo social reform, anti-nautch), and **Unnava Lakshminarayana** (*Malapalli*, social novel).
**Reading the pantheon:** they combined **language reform + social reform + literary modernism + nationalism** — the cultural engine of Andhra's self-assertion.
**Gidugu's revolution:** replacing the archaic *grandhika* with the living *vyavaharika* language democratised Telugu literacy and expression — a directly citable cultural-history point.
**Significance:** these makers turned a linguistic-cultural identity into the basis of a political demand for a Telugu-speaking state.

**First widow remarriage of coastal Andhra: 11 December 1881, Rajahmundry** (Kandukuri; groom Gogulapati Sriramulu).
Kandukuri's *Rajasekhara Charitramu* (1878) — pioneering Telugu novel; journal *Vivekavardhini* (1874); **Hitakarini Samaj** endowed with his estate.
***Kanyasulkam* premiered 1892 (Vizianagaram)**; enlarged edition 1909; characters Gireesham, Madhuravani — the anti-bride-price classic.
**Gurajada's 'Desamunu Preminchumanna' (1910)** — the Desabhakti anthem; court poet at **Vizianagaram**.
**Gidugu Ramamurthy**: Savara grammar (Munda linguistics pioneer); **Telugu Language Day: 29 August** (his birth anniversary).
Granthika champion opposing Gidugu: **Jayanti Ramayya Pantulu**.
**Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu** — Brahmo 'Kulapati' of Kakinada's Pithapuram Rajah's College; anti-nautch leader; knighted 1924.
Besant's Andhra lieutenants in Home Rule included **Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao** and **Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao**.

sections.heading: The library movement — reading rooms as nation-rooms

blocks.text: Andhra built India's most celebrated **library movement** — the conviction that a reading room in every village was self-rule's first institution. Milestones: early reading rooms (1870s-90s, reform era) → **Sri Krishnadevaraya Andhra Bhasha Nilayam (Hyderabad, 1901** — Komarraju Lakshmana Rao, Ravichettu Ranga Rao: the Telangana beacon) → **Vetapalem's Saraswata Niketanam (1918)** and hundreds of coastal libraries → **Andhra Desa Library Association (Andhradesa Grandhalaya Sangham), 1914 (Vijayawada)** — with its journal **Grandhalaya Sarvasvam (1916)** — → **All India Public Library Association (1919)** born of the Andhra impulse → the movement's statutory afterlife: the **Madras Public Libraries Act 1948 (S.R. Ranganathan's craftsmanship)** and **AP Public Libraries Act 1960**.

rows: **Leaders**

**Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya** — 'father of the library movement' (ADLA 1914, AIPLA 1919, Grandhalaya Sarvasvam); **Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao** — librarian-nationalist (also Vandemataram-era prisoner); **Komarraju Lakshmana Rao** — Hyderabad's Bhasha Nilayam + **Vignana Chandrika Grandhamala (1906**, popular-knowledge series) + the **Andhra Vignana Sarvasvamu** (first Telugu encyclopaedia project); Suri Venkata Narasimha Sastri, Vetapalem's founders
**Character**

Libraries doubled as **adult-literacy night schools, swadeshi platforms, khadi depots, harikatha-lecture venues**; travelling/boat libraries on the delta canals; women's reading sections — the library as the village's civic hall
**Politics**

Reading rooms hosted the **Andhra movement's** meetings and Congress campaigns; colonial CID watched them; during Non-Cooperation & CDM they were nationalism's nervous system — 'every library a fort of swaraj'

sections.heading: The newspaper estate — Telugu journalism's political work

items: **The genealogy** (building on HCOI-030): *Vivekavardhini* (1874, reform) → **Krishna Patrika (1902, Machilipatnam; Mutnuri Krishna Rao's** philosophical-nationalist editorship) → **Andhra Patrika (Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao**; Bombay weekly 1908 → Madras daily 1914; the **Bharati (1924)** literary monthly and **Andhra Grandhamala**) → Gadicherla's **Swarajya** (1908 'Viplavam' prosecution) → Prakasam's **Swarajya (1922, Madras** — trilingual daily of the NCM era) → regional papers (Zamin Ryot, Nellore 1930; Golconda Patrika, Hyderabad — Suravaram Pratapareddy) → **Andhra Prabha (1938)** and the modern press.

**Functions performed**: made 'Andhra' a daily-imagined community (the papers campaigned explicitly for **separate Andhra province** and for **university, ports, irrigation**); translated national movements into Telugu idiom; built the reform-literature public (Bharati's canon-making); financed and staffed the Congress machine (Kasinathuni — 'Desoddharaka', the nation-lifter — bankrolled movement and medicine alike: Amrutanjan's founder).

**Assessment**: library + newspaper = the **infrastructure of Andhra identity** — before the Andhra movement had institutions, it had reading rooms and dailies; the 1914 ADLA predates Andhra Mahasabha's key phase — civil society preceded and produced the political demand: the note's thesis.

sections.heading: 🏺 Deep mastery — the library & newspaper movements

items: **The library (Granthalaya) movement:** reading rooms as engines of literacy, awareness and nationalism; **Ayyanki Venkata Ramanaiah** organised the Andhra library movement — libraries as 'people's universities'.

**The Telugu press:** journals and newspapers (**Krishna Patrika, Andhra Patrika — Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao 'Desoddharaka'**) built public opinion, promoted the language, and carried the national and Andhra-province message.
**Reading them together:** libraries + newspapers created a **Telugu public sphere** that underpinned the Andhra Mahasabha and the statehood movement.
**Significance:** cultural infrastructure (libraries, presses) was as vital as political agitation in forging Andhra identity.

prelimsPointers: **Ayyanki Venkata Ramanaiah** — father of the Andhra library movement.
**Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao** — founder of *Andhra Patrika*; titled 'Desoddharaka'.
**Sri Krishnadevaraya Andhra Bhasha Nilayam, Hyderabad — 1901** (Komarraju Lakshmana Rao et al.) — the movement's Telangana lighthouse.
**Andhradesa Grandhalaya Sangham (ADLA): 1914, Vijayawada — Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya**; journal **Grandhalaya Sarvasvam (1916)**.
**All India Public Library Association: 1919** — Andhra-initiated (Ayyanki its moving spirit).
**Saraswata Niketanam, Vetapalem (1918)** — the famed village library-archive of the Prakasam coast.
**Komarraju Lakshmana Rao**: **Vignana Chandrika Grandhamala (1906)**; pioneer of the Telugu encyclopaedia (**Andhra Vignana Sarvasvamu**).

**Mutnuri Krishna Rao** edited **Krishna Patrika (Machilipatnam, 1902–)**; **Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao ('Desoddharaka')** ran **Andhra Patrika** (daily 1914) & **Bharati (1924)** — also founded **Amrutanjan (1893)**.
**Prakasam's Swarajya (1922)** — Madras trilingual nationalist daily.
Library laws: **Madras Public Libraries Act 1948** (Ranganathan's five laws lineage); **AP Public Libraries Act 1960**.
